```{r}
#| label: setup
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(knitr); library(kableExtra); library(ggplot2); library(scales)
})
res <- readRDS("results/res.rds")
repo_url <- ""   # GitHub repository of the group (to be filled in by the authors; printed in Appendix C when not empty)
neg <- function(x) sub("^-", "\\\\textminus{}", x)                               # typographic minus sign (LaTeX)
p2 <- function(x, d = 2) neg(sub("^-(0\\.?0*)$", "\\1", formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d)))   # percent
f2 <- function(x, d = 2) neg(sub("^-(0\\.?0*)$", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)))         # no "-0.00"
pv <- function(p) ifelse(is.na(p), "", ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", ifelse(p < 0.1, formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3),
                                                                           formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 2))))
mdate <- function(m) as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", m %/% 12L, m %% 12L + 1L))   # first day of month m
eom <- function(m) mdate(m + 1L) - 1                                               # last day of month m
ym <- function(y, m) y * 12L + m - 1L                                              # month id, as in build.R
row_of <- function(dt, name) dt[strategy == name]
s <- res$series; cfg <- res$cfg
in_p <- function(m, p) m >= p[1] & m <= p[2]
theme_paper <- theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey90", linewidth = 0.3),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 8), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8.5))
pal <- c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#4a3aa7", "#52514e")   # low beta, high beta, L-H, beta neutral, market/benchmark
col_mv <- "#c2185b"; col_ew <- "#eda100"; col_buf <- "#86b6ef"     # minimum variance, 1/N, buffer rule (same colours in every figure)
nw_l <- function(n) floor(4 * (n / 100)^(2 / 9))                   # Newey-West rule-of-thumb lag, as nw_lag() in R/functions.R
log_breaks <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500)
ramp5 <- c("#86b6ef", "#5598e7", "#2a78d6", "#1c5cab", "#0d366b")
nber <- data.table(start = as.Date(c("1929-08-01","1937-05-01","1945-02-01","1948-11-01","1953-07-01",
  "1957-08-01","1960-04-01","1969-12-01","1973-11-01","1980-01-01","1981-07-01","1990-07-01",
  "2001-03-01","2007-12-01","2020-02-01")), end = as.Date(c("1933-03-01","1938-06-01","1945-10-01",
  "1949-10-01","1954-05-01","1958-04-01","1961-02-01","1970-11-01","1975-03-01","1980-07-01",
  "1982-11-01","1991-03-01","2001-11-01","2009-06-01","2020-04-01")))
tab <- function(df, caption, label, notes = NULL, align = NULL, fs = 8.5, header = NULL, wide = FALSE) {
  k <- kbl(df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, caption = caption, label = label,
           align = align, linesep = "") |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", if (wide) "scale_down"), font_size = fs, position = "center")
  if (!is.null(header)) k <- add_header_above(k, header, escape = TRUE, bold = FALSE)
  if (!is.null(notes)) k <- footnote(k, general = notes, general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
  k
}
interleave <- function(est, tst, lab) {   # estimates with t-statistics underneath
  out <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(est))) {
    out[[2 * i - 1]] <- cbind(lab[i], est[i, ])
    out[[2 * i]] <- cbind("", as.data.frame(lapply(tst[i, ], function(x) ifelse(is.na(x) | x == "", "", paste0("(", x, ")")))))
  }
  rbindlist(lapply(out, as.data.table), use.names = FALSE)
}
states_lab <- c("1 (low)", "2", "3", "4", "5 (high)")
cl <- function(x, d) formatC(ceiling(x * 10^d) / 10^d, format = "f", digits = d)   # upper bound at d decimals
andlist <- function(v) if (length(v) <= 1) as.character(v) else paste(paste(v[-length(v)], collapse = ", "), "and", v[length(v)])
```

```{r}
#| label: facts
# ---- every number quoted in the text is taken from res; qualitative claims are checked below ----
T1 <- res$T1
gfk_t1 <- data.table(strategy = c("Q1","Q2","Q3","Q4","Q5","Low - high","Beta neutral","Market"),
  arith = c(.89,.92,.86,.85,.73,.16,.71,.87), geo = c(.83,.84,.75,.70,.47,-.02,.67,.76),
  beta = c(.47,.76,.98,1.24,1.76,-1.29,.03,1.00), sharpe = c(.45,.42,.32,.27,.15,.10,.46,.33))
cmp <- merge(T1, gfk_t1, by = "strategy", suffixes = c("", "_p"))
gap_bp <- mean(abs(100 * cmp$arith - cmp$arith_p)) * 100
gap_beta <- max(abs(cmp$beta_ante - cmp$beta))
gap_sr <- max(abs(cmp$sharpe - cmp$sharpe_p))
q <- function(tb, st, v) tb[strategy == st][[v]]
A <- res$T2A
B2 <- res$T2BC
B <- dcast(B2[h > 1], strategy + state ~ h, value.var = "value")
b12 <- function(stg, st) B[strategy == stg & state == st, `12`]
b60 <- function(stg, st) B[strategy == stg & state == st, `60`]
tb <- function(stg, st, hh = 12) B2[strategy == stg & state == st & h == hh, t_boot]
ci <- function(stg, st, hh = 12) { z <- B2[strategy == stg & state == st & h == hh]; 100 * (z$value + c(-1.96, 1.96) * z$se_boot) }
# GFKSW Table 3 (their p. 55-56): average window alphas (% per month) and t-statistics at t+12 and t+60, states 1-5
gfk3 <- list(
  LH = list(capm = cbind(a12 = c(.07,.45,-.11,.46,1.04), t12 = c(.10,.90,-.34,2.62,5.11), a60 = c(.14,.36,.37,.39,.92), t60 = c(1.15,1.23,2.25,2.69,4.28)),
            f4   = cbind(a12 = c(.10,.18,.03,.06,.40), t12 = c(.31,.66,.16,.24,1.86), a60 = c(.22,.15,-.11,-.09,.29), t60 = c(1.30,.72,-.67,-.58,1.72))),
  BN = list(capm = cbind(a12 = c(.00,.15,-.09,.27,.68), t12 = c(-.01,.44,-.51,2.56,5.09), a60 = c(.02,.15,.21,.23,.52), t60 = c(.18,.67,2.07,2.91,4.07)),
            f4   = cbind(a12 = c(.03,.04,-.01,.06,.34), t12 = c(.19,.20,-.07,.29,1.85), a60 = c(.11,.06,-.07,-.06,.16), t60 = c(.91,.39,-.64,-.53,1.02))))
# GFKSW Table 2, Panel A: B/P spread range and average number of stocks per extreme quintile by state
gfk2a <- data.table(state = 1:5, from = c(-.55,-.01,.12,.22,.27), to = c(-.01,.12,.22,.27,.59), n = c(104,101,108,106,94))
gB <- list(LH = rbind(c(-5.80,-3.63,-3.37,-3.29,-2.83), c(4.64,-.67,.24,.33,.24), c(-6.84,-5.30,-3.99,-2.50,-2.23),
                      c(3.36,1.62,-2.45,-3.11,-2.81), c(12.52,8.45,6.45,4.96,4.40)),
           BN = rbind(c(2.30,3.71,3.06,1.04,1.62), c(3.97,1.51,2.06,2.47,2.61), c(2.53,2.28,3.31,3.74,3.49),
                      c(5.63,4.73,4.09,4.35,4.34), c(10.27,10.42,9.25,8.99,9.10)))
D51 <- res$boot_d51
d51 <- function(stg, v = "d_ret", hh = 12) D51[strategy == stg & h == hh][[v]]
d51ci <- function(stg, hh = 12) 100 * (d51(stg, "d_ret", hh) + c(-1.96, 1.96) * d51(stg, "se_d_ret", hh))
LD <- res$lodo
ld <- function(dec, v) if (is.na(dec)) LD[is.na(dropped)][[v]] else LD[dropped == dec][[v]]
ld_range <- function(v) range(LD[!is.na(dropped)][[v]])
ld_dec <- function(v, f) { z <- LD[!is.na(dropped)]; z$dropped[f(z[[v]])] }
wid_lh <- B2[strategy == "LH" & h == 12, 2 * 1.96 * 100 * se_boot]
SI <- res$sim_inference[, lapply(.SD, mean), keyby = h, .SDcols = c("rej_gfksw", "rej_hac", "rej_boot")]

               amv = mean(a_mv > 0), vol = mean(vol_lb < vol_vw), volmv = mean(vol_mv < vol_vw),

# v4: checks of the inference for the state averages and the central contrast (Section 3.3, Appendix Tables inf and size)
BC <- res$boot_checks
bc <- function(stg, meth, blk, v, st = "d51", hh = 12L) BC[strategy == stg & method == meth & block == blk & h == hh & stat == st][[v]]
t_rng <- function(stg) range(BC[strategy == stg & method == "null" & h == 12 & stat == "d51", t])
SCt <- res$sim_contrast

SV <- res$state_vol; DEP <- res$dependence
sv <- function(stg, st) SV[strategy == stg & state == st, realised]
se_lh <- B2[strategy == "LH" & h == 12, 100 * se_boot]
# v4: daily return paths from CRSP's daily file (Section 8, Appendix Table daily)
RCv <- res$recon[strategy == "Large-cap VW"]
rcn <- function(cl) { x <- RCv[cls == cl, stock_months]; if (length(x)) x else 0L }
dvv <- res$daily_variants

# ---- claim checks: rendering stops if a statement in the text is no longer supported ----------
# (they flag text that must be rewritten after a recomputation; they never change a calculation)
chk <- function(cond, msg) if (!isTRUE(all(cond))) stop("Claim no longer supported by results: ", msg)
chk(dd$check_cm_vs_msf$max_abs_diff == 0 && dd$check_cm_vs_msf$cm_rows_without_msf == 0, "crsp_monthly returns identical to msf_v2")
chk(dd$hold_check$no_return_in_samples == 0 && dd$hold_check$no_trade_from_1967_12 == 0, "no missing holding return in the samples; no-trade months only before 1968")
chk(max(abs(imp[variant == "v2", lh] - imp[variant == "v3", lh])) < 1e-4, "delisting fix changes the mean L-H return by less than 1 bp")
chk(gap_bp < 2 && gap_beta < 0.05, "Table 1 matches GFKSW to within 2 bp on average, betas within 0.05")
chk(b12("LH", 5) > 0 && b12("LH", 1) < 0 && abs(100 * b12("LH", 5) - 12.52) < 1.5 && abs(100 * b12("LH", 1) + 5.80) < 1.5,
    "L-H 12m close to GFKSW in states 1 and 5")
chk(abs(100 * b12("BN", 5) - 10.27) < 1 && abs(100 * b12("BN", 1) - 2.30) > 1, "BN state 5 matches, state 1 does not")
bn_neg <- B[strategy == "BN"][, .(state, `24`, `36`)]
chk(all(B[strategy == "BN", `12`] > 0) && sum(B[strategy == "BN", c(`12`, `24`, `36`, `48`, `60`)] < 0) == 2 &&
    bn_neg[state == 2, `24` < 0 & `36` < 0], "BN positive after every state at one year; negative only after state 2 at two and three years")
chk(b12("BN", 5) == max(B[strategy == "BN", `12`]), "BN 12m highest in state 5")
chk(identical(B2[strategy == "LH" & h == 12 & abs(t_boot) > 1.96, state], 5L) && identical(B2[strategy == "BN" & h == 12 & abs(t_boot) > 1.96, state], 4:5),
    "bootstrap: one-year means significant only in state 5 (L-H) and states 4-5 (BN)")
chk(res$T5[state == 5 & h == 12, value] == max(res$T5[h == 12, value]) && res$T5[state == 5 & h == 36, value] < 0 && res$T5[state == 1 & h == 12, value] < 0,
    "1930-2012: state 5 best first year, negative from three years; state 1 negative")
chk(W[h == 60, median(abs(t_gfk_capm) / abs(t_boot_capm))] > W[h == 12, median(abs(t_gfk_capm) / abs(t_boot_capm))] &&
    W[h == 12, median(abs(t_boot_capm) / abs(t_gfk_capm))] <= 1, "bootstrap t mostly smaller at one year, gap larger at five years")
chk(all(abs(c(d51("LH", "t_d_ret"), d51("BN", "t_d_ret")) - 1.96) < 0.3), "state 5 - state 1 contrast: t close to the 5% threshold for L-H and BN")
chk(d51("LH", "t_d_ret", 60) < 1 && d51("LH", "t_d_ret", 36) < 1.645, "contrast insignificant at three and five years")
chk(ld(2000L, "lh12") < 0.25 * ld(NA, "lh12") && ld(1980L, "a5_lh") < 0.25 * ld(NA, "a5_lh"), "single decades dominate the central results")
chk(si(12, "rej_boot") < 0.08 && si(60, "rej_boot") < 0.08 && si(12, "rej_gfksw") > 0.10 && si(60, "rej_gfksw") > 0.25,
    "bootstrap close to nominal size; GFKSW-style statistic over-rejects")
chk(max(abs(W$t_boot_4f)) < 1.96, "no four-factor window alpha significant with the bootstrap")
chk(all(W[state == 5, t_boot_capm] > 1.96), "state-5 CAPM alphas significant at every horizon (bootstrap)")
chk(w_("LH", 1, 60, "t_gfk_4f") > 3 && abs(w_("LH", 1, 60, "t_boot_4f")) < 1.96, "state-1 60m four-factor alpha: GFKSW-style t > 3, bootstrap insignificant")
chk(max(abs(CT$t_4f)) < 1.96 && all(CT[state == 5, t_capm] > 1.96), "calendar-time alternative: same pattern")
chk(cnt("post", 4) == 0 && cnt("post", 5) == 0 && rcnt("post", 4) == 0 && rcnt("post", 5) == 0, "no post-2012 month in states 4-5")
chk(pf("post", "LH", "mean_ex") < 0 && pf("post", "BN", "mean_ex") > 0 && pf("pub", "LH", "mean_ex") < 0 && pf("pub", "BN", "mean_ex") > 0,
    "post-sample L-H negative, BN positive")
chk(abs(pf("post", "Q1", "t_capm")) < 1.96 && abs(pf("pub", "Q1", "t_capm")) < 1.96, "Q1 CAPM alpha insignificant after 2012")
chk(all(srq[period %in% c("post", "pub"), p] > 0.10), "Q1 vs market Sharpe difference insignificant after 2012")
chk(pf("post", "Q1", "sharpe") < pf("post", "MKT", "sharpe"), "Q1 Sharpe below market since 2013")
chk(tmr("post", "LH", "val", "invested") == 0 && tmr("pub", "LH", "val", "invested") == 0, "timing rule never invested after 2012")
chk(tmr("full", "BN", "val", "sharpe_net") < tmr("full", "BN", "always", "sharpe_net"), "timing lowers BN net Sharpe")
chk(tmr("full", "LH", "always", "sharpe_net") < 0 && tmr("full", "LH", "val", "sharpe_net") > 0, "timing turns L-H net Sharpe positive")
chk(all(tm[period == "full" & !is.na(p_holm), p_holm] > 0.10), "no significant timing improvement")
chk(dmv("beta_D36", "beta_M60", "dm_t") < 0 && dmv("beta_D36", "beta_M60", "p_holm") < 0.05 && dmv("beta_DD12", "beta_M60", "p_holm") < 0.05,
    "D36 and DD12 forecasts significantly better than M60")
chk(dmv("beta_D36", "beta_M36", "dm_t") < -1.96, "frequency effect at a 36-month window")
chk(dmv("beta_M36", "beta_M60", "dm_t") > 1.96 && dmv("beta_D3", "beta_D36", "dm_t") > 1.96 && abs(dmv("beta_D12", "beta_D36", "dm_t")) < 1.96,
    "window effects: short windows worse")
chk(all(srb$p_holm > 0.10), "no significant strategy difference across beta estimators")
chk(xA[spec == "beta_M60", val_effect] == max(xA$val_effect) && xA[spec == "beta_M60", bnd_sharpe] == max(xA$bnd_sharpe),
    "M60 has the largest valuation effect and BN Sharpe ratio")
chk(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta")$sr_diff > 0 && row_of(LOn, "LowBeta")$p_sr > 0.10, "small insignificant net Sharpe advantage")
chk(all(LOn[strategy %in% c("LowBeta", "LowBeta buffer", "LowBeta quarterly", "LowBeta (daily 12m)", "Min-variance", "Large-cap EW"), p_holm] > 0.10),
    "no Holm-significant long-only Sharpe difference")
chk(row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$vol < row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$vol && row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$mdd < row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$mdd &&
    row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$mean_ex < row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$mean_ex, "low beta: lower risk, lower excess return")
chk(row_of(LOp, "LowBeta")$sr_diff < 0, "Q1 net Sharpe below benchmark 2013-2024")
chk(row_of(LO, "Min-variance")$alpha_capm == max(LO[strategy != "Market (FF)", alpha_capm]) &&
    row_of(LOn, "Min-variance")$sharpe == max(LOn[strategy != "Market (FF)", sharpe]), "min-variance: largest CAPM alpha and net Sharpe ratio")
chk(row_of(BE, "LowBeta buffer")$be_sr == max(BE$be_sr, na.rm = TRUE), "buffer rule has the highest break-even cost")
chk(abs(row_of(dv, "LowBeta")$dv_pct - row_of(dv, "Large-cap VW")$dv_pct) < 0.05 && row_of(dv, "Min-variance")$dv_pct < row_of(dv, "LowBeta")$dv_pct,
    "low beta as liquid as the benchmark by dollar-volume rank; min-var less")
```

```{=latex}
\begin{abstract}
```
Can investors build a robust, implementable strategy on the low-beta anomaly? @gfksw2015 [hereafter GFKSW] argue that it is cyclical: low-beta stocks beat high-beta stocks only when they start out cheap, and value and momentum absorb much of the conditional alpha. Rebuilding their study from CRSP and Compustat, we reproduce their unconditional results almost exactly and the zero-cost portfolio's one-year returns after the extreme valuation states, but not the middle states. The cheap-minus-expensive contrasts are not robustly significant at the 5% level. A bias-corrected predictive regression, which tests a different hypothesis (a linear relation between spread and next-year return), indicates in sample that the spread predicts the beta-neutral portfolio's return ($t$ = `r f2(ahv("rep", "BN", "ah_t"))`). The conditional premium coincides with a value exposure; its four-factor alphas are insignificant under our bootstraps. Since 2013, valuations have never been cheap enough to test the central prediction. For long-only investors, the `r p2(short_share, 0)`% of the zero-cost portfolio's CAPM alpha that comes from shorting high-beta stocks is out of reach: low-beta portfolios cut volatility by about a fifth but do not beat the cap-weighted benchmark significantly (net Sharpe ratio `r f2(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta")$sharpe)` against `r f2(row_of(LOn, "Large-cap VW")$sharpe)`, $p$ = `r pv(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta")$p_sr)`), and the daily nonlinear-shrinkage minimum-variance portfolio has the lowest realized volatility of all portfolios but, after costs, a net Sharpe ratio no higher than the simple low-beta quintile's.

```{=latex}
\end{abstract}

\newpage
```
# Introduction

Since @bjs1972 documented that the security market line is too flat and @black1972 explained it with borrowing restrictions, a large literature has shown that low-risk stocks earn risk-adjusted returns above, and raw returns at least equal to, those of high-risk stocks [@ang2006; @blitz2007; @baker2011; @frazzini2014]. The finding contradicts the most basic prediction of the CAPM and underlies minimum-volatility indices and low-beta funds; whether investors can capture it in a robust, implementable strategy is our question.

@gfksw2015 qualify this evidence on three counts. First, the conventional zero-cost portfolio that is long the lowest-beta and short the highest-beta quintile carries a market beta of about $-1.3$; shorting only a quarter of the high-beta quintile removes most of this exposure. Second, the premium is cyclical: the lowest-risk portfolio outperforms "only when valuation is strongly in its favor" [@gfksw2015, p. 54], that is, when the book-to-price ratio of low-beta stocks is high relative to that of high-beta stocks by historical standards. Third, much of the conditional CAPM alpha disappears once value and momentum are controlled for. They do not propose a timing rule, and their sample ends in December 2012.

We ask whether the valuation dependence of the low-beta premium is a robust feature that an investor can use or an in-sample pattern resting on a few episodes. We answer in three steps: we rebuild GFKSW's study from the raw data and test its central contrast with inference that respects overlapping windows; we follow the strategies to 2024; and we ask what an investor can capture once beta has to be estimated, short sales are restricted, trading costs are paid and performance is judged at daily frequency and over rolling windows.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it separates what replicates from what does not: GFKSW's unconditional results and the one-year returns after the extreme states reproduce, their middle states do not, and, in our reconstruction and simulations, their Newey-West statistics overstate the precision of averages over overlapping windows. The cheap-minus-expensive contrasts are not robustly significant at the 5% level. That of the zero-cost portfolio rests largely on the technology bust and the 2009 rebound, and the conditional premium coincides largely with a value exposure. A bias-corrected predictive regression, testing the different hypothesis of a linear relation between spread and next-year return, finds in sample that the spread predicts the beta-neutral portfolio's return. Second, a CAPM decomposition attributes the negative post-sample excess returns of the zero-cost portfolio mainly to its negative market beta in a rising market, while valuations never reached the states in which GFKSW expect low-beta stocks to win. Third, it quantifies the gap between the academic factor and an investable portfolio: most of the premium comes from the short side, a long-only low-beta portfolio offers lower risk but no significant net Sharpe ratio gain, better beta forecasts bring no significant gain in gross Sharpe ratios, and the daily nonlinear-shrinkage portfolio has the lowest realized volatility but no higher net Sharpe ratio.

Sections 2 and 3 cover literature and methods, Section 4 the replication, Section 5 post-sample performance and timing, Sections 6 to 8 the implementation, and Section 9 concludes.

# Related literature

Risk-based explanations of the low-risk anomaly build on @black1972: investors who cannot or will not borrow tilt towards high-beta stocks, which flattens the security market line [@frazzini2014]. Institutional explanations stress benchmarking: managers measured against a cap-weighted index have little incentive to hold low-beta stocks that raise tracking error [@baker2011]. Low-risk investing works within and across industries [@asness2014], limits to arbitrage concentrate the anomaly in small, illiquid stocks [@li2014], one reason GFKSW restrict attention to large caps, and much of the betting-against-beta premium depends on construction choices such as beta shrinkage and equal weighting [@novymarx2022]. The role of value and momentum relates to the factor models of @fama1993 and @carhart1997 and to the fragility of momentum [@daniel2016]; timing factors with their own valuation spreads has been hard in practice [@asness2017].

For the implementation analyses, @hollstein2019 find that betas from daily returns forecast future betas better than five-year monthly estimates, and @dimson1979 corrects daily betas for non-synchronous trading. Many anomalies do not survive trading costs [@novymarx2016; @denard2022], long-only implementations can be preferable once costs and constraints are considered [@blitz2014], the $1/N$ portfolio is a hard benchmark [@demiguel2009], and shrinkage makes minimum-variance portfolios usable in large cross-sections [@ledoit2004; @clarke2006; @ledoit2020]. Published anomalies weaken after publication [@mclean2016], significance thresholds should rise with the number of tests [@harvey2016], and carefully replicated factors largely survive [@jensen2023].

# Data and methodology

## Data

Monthly and daily returns of US common stocks traded on NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ come from CRSP via the university's Tidy Finance database [@tidyfinance2023], in CRSP's current (CIZ) format. Holding-period returns come from CRSP's monthly security file, which keeps the month in which a stock delists and includes the delisting return in that month's total return; stocks whose last trading day falls in the formation month are not bought. Every held stock therefore has a return.[^1] GFKSW instead set the delisting return, not the whole month's return, of performance-related delistings to $-30$% (NYSE, AMEX) or $-55$% (NASDAQ), following @shumway1997. In our large-cap universe, a held stock was dropped by its exchange in only `r gfk_rep` stock-months of 1968--2012 (`r gfk_n` over 1929--2024), `r c("none", "one", "two")[gfk_ext + 1]` of them in an extreme beta quintile, so applying their rule leaves the mean low-minus-high return unchanged to within 0.01 basis points (Appendix Table \ref{tab:a1}). In our sample, the delisting treatments tested do not explain differences from their results.

[^1]: Over 1968--2012, delisting months carry on average `r f2(100 * min(dd$q_rep$w_msf), 2)`% to `r f2(100 * max(dd$q_rep$w_msf), 2)`% of a beta quintile's weight, the formation-month exclusions `r f2(100 * min(dd$q_rep$w_excl), 2)`% to `r f2(100 * max(dd$q_rep$w_excl), 2)`%. Dropping the delisting months instead changes the mean low-minus-high return by `r f2(1e4 * abs(im("rep", "v3", "lh") - im("rep", "v2", "lh")), 2)` basis points per month (Appendix Table \ref{tab:a1}).

Book equity follows @fama1992 and uses only December fiscal year-ends with at least two years of Compustat history, as in GFKSW; before Compustat coverage we use the book equity of @davis2000, GFKSW's source for the years before 1951. Factors and the one-month T-bill rate are from Kenneth French's data library [@frenchlib]; GFKSW use three-month T-bills. Instead of the CRSP value-weighted index, we use the Fama--French market total return (MKT--RF + RF), whose mean over 1968--2012 matches our panel's value-weighted return (both `r f2(100 * dd$mkt_ff, 3)`% per month; correlation `r f2(dd$mkt_cor, 3)`). Regressions use the market excess return, MKT--RF. The momentum factor ends in December 2024, which ends every sample. Daily betas use CRSP's daily returns; the daily portfolio paths of Section 8 also use the delisting-day records of CRSP's daily file. GFKSW used the CRSP vintage of 2013, whose effect cannot be quantified here. Appendix Table \ref{tab:a0} compares the two designs.

## Portfolios and return definitions

At the end of each month $t$, each stock's CAPM beta is estimated from its excess returns over the previous 60 months (at least 24, including month $t$). The universe consists of stocks priced between USD 2 and USD 1,000 with a market capitalisation above the 67th percentile of NYSE stocks, on average `r f2(res$meta$n_large_rep, 0)` stocks per month in 1968--2012. Stocks are sorted into beta quintiles and held, value-weighted, over month $t+1$; all portfolios are rebalanced monthly unless stated otherwise.

All returns are total returns in USD; the excess return of a portfolio is its return minus the one-month T-bill rate $r_f$, and its active return is its return minus that of a benchmark. The low-minus-high portfolio (L--H) holds the investor's capital as collateral in T-bills and is long USD 1 of quintile 1 for every USD 1 of quintile 5 sold short, the short proceeds financing the long position. Its total return is $r_f + r_{Q1} - r_{Q5}$ and its excess return $r_{Q1} - r_{Q5}$. GFKSW's beta-neutral portfolio (BN) invests the capital in quintile 1 and shorts quintile 5 in an amount of 25% of capital, with the short proceeds in T-bills. Its total return is $r_{Q1} - 0.25\,r_{Q5} + 0.25\,r_f$ and its excess return $(r_{Q1} - r_f) - 0.25\,(r_{Q5} - r_f) = r_{Q1} - 0.25\,r_{Q5} - 0.75\,r_f$; the $0.75\,r_f$ term is the opportunity cost of the fully invested long position net of the interest on the short proceeds. Like GFKSW (their note 6), Table \ref{tab:t1} reports the raw return $r_{Q1} - 0.25\,r_{Q5}$ and computes Sharpe ratios from excess returns. These gross returns ignore lending fees and the spread between the rebate on short proceeds and the T-bill rate; net returns are defined in Section 3.4. The fixed short ratio of 25% matches GFKSW's full-sample average betas and therefore uses future information; we also reset it every month to $\hat\beta_{Q1,t}/\hat\beta_{Q5,t}$ (BN ex ante) and, as @frazzini2014 do, to the same ratio with betas shrunk towards one, $0.6\hat\beta + 0.4$ (BN shrunk).

For horizons of $h$ months we compound the monthly excess returns of the monthly rebalanced strategy, $\prod_{k=1}^{h}(1+x_{t+k})-1$, and annualise geometrically. This compounds monthly excess returns and is distinct from the total-return wealth paths in @fig-cum; GFKSW rebalance monthly (their notes 9 and 10) but do not state how they compound. Relative wealth of two buy-and-hold portfolios and the payoff of a never-rebalanced long-short position answer different questions (Appendix Table \ref{tab:a2}).

## Valuation states and inference

The B/P spread is the average book-to-price ratio of quintile 1 minus that of quintile 5, with December book equity of year $y-1$ used from the end of June of year $y$ and market value measured at the end of the formation month [@asness2013]. The higher the spread, the cheaper low-beta stocks are relative to high-beta stocks; because the spread is positive in most months, "cheap" and "expensive" below always mean relative to the spread's own history. GFKSW "deleted the top and bottom 0.5% of the B/P observations" but report 540 months with 108 per state; we therefore read the trimming as applying to stock-level ratios, not months, and trim each month's cross-section of large-cap B/P ratios at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles, which uses no future information. The 540 formation months from December 1967 to November 2012 (return months January 1968 to December 2012) are sorted into spread quintiles ("states"): state 5 is the cheapest fifth for low-beta stocks, state 1 the most expensive. As in GFKSW, these breakpoints use the whole sample; Section 5 also uses breakpoints estimated in real time. Only windows that end by December 2012 enter the replication (state 1 keeps `r n_win[h == 12, n]` of 108 windows at one year and `r n_win[h == 60, n]` at five years).

Tables \ref{tab:t2bc} and \ref{tab:t3} average, for every state, a statistic computed over the $h$ months after each formation month: the annualised chained excess return, or the intercept of a CAPM or four-factor regression. Where we replicate GFKSW's tables we also report their statistic as we read it, a Newey-West $t$ with $h$ lags on the state-filtered sequence of window estimates. Overlapping windows and states that cluster in a few episodes make that sequence strongly dependent. Our baseline is therefore a block bootstrap. We cut the monthly history of strategy and factor returns into blocks of `r res$boot_info$block` months, draw blocks with replacement, wrapping around the end of the sample [@kunsch1989; @politis1992], keep the dates of the valuation signals fixed and recompute every state average (`r res$boot_info$B` draws). Because the reshuffled returns are unrelated to the signals, the draws show how far apart the state averages fall by chance when the states carry no information; their standard deviation gives the $t$-statistics and their centred quantiles the $p$-values, not confidence intervals. Blocks of 24 months lie between the `r f2(DEP[strategy == "LH", pw_block], 0)` months that the rule of [@politis2004; corrected by @patton2009] selects for the mean of the L--H returns and the `r f2(DEP[strategy == "LH", pw_block_sq], 0)` months it selects for their squares; Appendix Table \ref{tab:inf} reports blocks of 12 to 60 months.

The bootstrap assumes that volatility is unrelated to the signal dates, which fails here: in the year after a state-5 month the L--H volatility averages `r p2(sv("LH", 5), 0)`% per year, against `r p2(min(SV[strategy == "LH" & state < 5, realised]), 0)`% to `r p2(max(SV[strategy == "LH" & state < 5, realised]), 0)`% after the other states. A volatility-preserving variant therefore rescales the reshuffled, standardised returns with the local volatility of the original dates. Size simulations with the actual state calendar (Appendix Table \ref{tab:size}) show that the 24-month bootstrap rejects a true null at the 5% level in `r f2(rej_rng("null24", c("state5", "d51"))[1], 1)`% to `r f2(rej_rng("null24", c("state5", "d51"))[2], 1)`% of the samples when volatility is unrelated to the calendar, the GFKSW-style statistic in `r f2(rej_rng("gfksw_nw", "state5")[1], 1)`% to `r f2(rej_rng("gfksw_nw", "state5")[2], 1)`%. Under the observed volatility path the baseline bootstrap over-rejects, most for the state-5 means (Appendix Table \ref{tab:size}); for the L--H contrast its size-adjusted 5% critical value is `r f2(sct("LH", "observed_vol", "null24", "d51", "crit95"))`, that of the volatility-preserving variant `r f2(sct("LH", "observed_vol", "vp24", "d51", "crit95"))`. No procedure can overcome the small number of episodes. Calendar-time regressions on stacked windows estimate a different quantity and are reported in Appendix Table \ref{tab:a5}.

A predictive regression of the next year's return on the standardised spread avoids classifying months into states. The spread is persistent and its innovations correlate with returns, inducing small-sample OLS bias [@stambaugh1999]; we therefore report the reduced-bias estimator of @amihud2004 on non-overlapping December observations.

The extensions use Newey-West $t$-statistics with the rule-of-thumb lag $\lfloor 4(T/100)^{2/9}\rfloor$ [@newey1987]. Sharpe ratios are compared with the HAC test of @ledoit2008 on the common sample, beta forecasts with Diebold-Mariano tests, and within each family of comparisons with a common benchmark we report Holm-adjusted $p$-values [@harvey2016]. Three analyses are primary: the replication, the performance after 2012, and the comparison of the long-only low-beta quintile with the cap-weighted benchmark after costs (one test, unadjusted). Everything else is exploratory.

## Costs, turnover and liquidity

Turnover at a rebalancing date is $\sum_i |w_{i,t} - \tilde w_{i,t}|$, where $\tilde w$ are the previous target weights after drifting with returns over the holding period. It counts purchases and sales, so a one-way cost $c$ per dollar traded is charged as $c$ times turnover; a stock that delisted during the month counts as a sale. Every portfolio, including each benchmark, bears costs on its own turnover. The base case of $c = 10$ basis points is the flat cost used by @denard2022 and twice the cost they assume for large caps; because we have no transaction-level data, 0 to 50 basis points are reported as scenarios. Short positions pay a lending fee of 25 basis points per year on the short notional, the value-weighted borrowing cost of the loan portfolio studied by @davolio2002 (17 basis points for the 91% of lent stocks that are cheap to borrow); this, too, is a scenario value, not calibrated to our sample. The cost model ignores market impact, financing spreads and the possibility that a stock cannot be borrowed. CRSP reports trading volume, which we use only to describe the liquidity of each portfolio (Section 7); we have no data on market impact or borrowing availability.

# Replication

## Risk, return and the construction of the long-short portfolio

```{r}
#| label: tab-t1
t1 <- copy(T1)[strategy != "Beta neutral (ex ante)"]
t1 <- merge(t1, gfk_t1, by = "strategy", suffixes = c("", "_p"), sort = FALSE)
ord <- c("Q1","Q2","Q3","Q4","Q5","Low - high","Beta neutral","Market")
t1 <- t1[match(ord, strategy)]
lab <- c("1 (low)", "2", "3", "4", "5 (high)", "Low -- high", "Beta neutral", "Market")
tst <- ifelse(t1$strategy %in% c("Low - high", "Beta neutral", "Market"), paste0(" (", f2(t1$t), ")"), "")
df <- data.frame(Portfolio = lab,
  a = paste0(f2(100 * t1$arith), tst), ap = f2(t1$arith_p),
  g = f2(100 * t1$geo), gp = f2(t1$geo_p),
  b = f2(t1$beta_ante), bp = f2(t1$beta), br = f2(t1$beta_real),
  s = f2(t1$sharpe), sp = f2(t1$sharpe_p))
names(df) <- c("Beta quintile", "Ours", "GFKSW", "Ours", "GFKSW", "Ours", "GFKSW", "Realised", "Ours", "GFKSW")
tab(df, "Risk and return of beta-sorted portfolios, January 1968 to December 2012 (replication of GFKSW Table 1)", "t1",
    notes = paste0("Value-weighted monthly raw returns in percent of large-cap stocks sorted on 60-month CAPM betas; ",
      "ordinary t-statistics in parentheses, as in GFKSW. Beta: average pre-formation beta; Realised: slope of the portfolio's monthly ",
      "excess return on the market excess return. Sharpe ratios are annualised and use excess returns ",
      "(L--H: $r_{Q1}-r_{Q5}$; beta neutral: $r_{Q1}-0.25\\\\,r_{Q5}-0.75\\\\,r_f$). The beta-neutral mean is the raw return ",
      "$r_{Q1}-0.25\\\\,r_{Q5}$. 540 months; GFKSW values from their Table 1."),
    align = "lrrrrrrrrr", fs = 8, header = c(" " = 1, "Arithmetic mean" = 2, "Geometric mean" = 2, "Beta" = 3, "Sharpe ratio" = 2))
```

Against the published values (Table \ref{tab:t1}), the average absolute difference in arithmetic means across the eight portfolios is `r f2(gap_bp, 1)` basis points per month, the pre-formation betas differ by at most `r f2(gap_beta, 2)` and the Sharpe ratios by at most `r f2(gap_sr, 2)`, and the $t$-statistics of the two long-short portfolios (`r f2(q(T1, "Low - high", "t"))` and `r f2(q(T1, "Beta neutral", "t"))`) are close to GFKSW's 0.63 and 5.49. Average returns are flat across the first four quintiles and fall in the highest-beta quintile, while Sharpe ratios fall from `r f2(q(T1, "Q1", "sharpe"))` to `r f2(q(T1, "Q5", "sharpe"))`. The L--H portfolio's mean excess return is `r f2(100 * q(T1, "Low - high", "arith"))`% per month and statistically insignificant; its market beta is `r f2(q(T1, "Low - high", "beta_ante"))` ex ante and `r f2(q(T1, "Low - high", "beta_real"))` ex post. The beta-neutral portfolio earns `r f2(100 * pf("rep", "BN", "mean_ex") / 12)`% per month in excess of T-bills ($t$ = `r f2(pf("rep", "BN", "t_ex"))`, Table \ref{tab:post}), the number comparable with L--H; the raw return of `r f2(100 * q(T1, "Beta neutral", "arith"))`% and its $t$ of `r f2(q(T1, "Beta neutral", "t"))`, which Table \ref{tab:t1} reports to match GFKSW, also contain three quarters of the T-bill return.

Neither portfolio is what its name suggests. Ex post, the quintile betas are compressed towards one, from `r f2(q(T1, "Q1", "beta_ante"))` to `r f2(q(T1, "Q1", "beta_real"))` for quintile 1 and from `r f2(q(T1, "Q5", "beta_ante"))` to `r f2(q(T1, "Q5", "beta_real"))` for quintile 5, as estimation error and mean reversion in beta imply. The beta-neutral portfolio therefore has a realised beta of `r f2(q(T1, "Beta neutral", "beta_real"))` (Newey-West standard error `r f2(q(T1, "Beta neutral", "beta_real_se"))`), and part of its return is ordinary equity premium. Shrinking the betas towards one before setting the short ratio, as @frazzini2014 do, raises the short position to `r f2(100 * mean(s[in_p(mid, cfg$rep), s_shr]), 0)`% of capital on average and lowers the realised beta to `r f2(pf("rep", "BNs", "beta"))` (1968--2024: `r f2(pf("full", "BNs", "beta"))`, Appendix Table \ref{tab:ls}). Restricting the universe to firms with a December book value barely changes the extreme quintiles and the long-short portfolios of Table \ref{tab:t1}, although it reorders the mean returns of the middle quintiles (Appendix Table \ref{tab:a4}).

Panel (a): value-weighted lowest- and highest-beta quintiles of the large-cap universe and the Fama-French market. Panel (b): the low-minus-high portfolio (capital in T-bills, long Q1 and short Q5: $r_f + r_{Q1} - r_{Q5}$), the beta-neutral portfolio ($r_{Q1} - 0.25\\,r_{Q5} + 0.25\\,r_f$), the market and T-bills. @fig-cum shows how the construction shapes realised wealth. One dollar invested in January 1968 grew to `r f2(tw("ret1"), 0)` dollars in the low-beta quintile, `r f2(tw("ret5"), 0)` in the high-beta quintile and `r f2(tw("mkt", TRUE), 0)` in the market by December 2024. The dollar-neutral L--H portfolio ended at `r f2(tw("LH", TRUE), 1)` dollars, below the `r f2(tw("rf"), 1)` of T-bills; the beta-neutral portfolio ended at `r f2(tw("BN", TRUE), 0)` dollars. Appendix Table \ref{tab:ls} reports their mean excess returns and CAPM decompositions.

## Valuation cycles

```{r}
#| label: spread-facts
neg_years <- s[spread < 0 & fmid >= ym(1967L, 12L), unique(fmid %/% 12L)]
chk(any(neg_years %in% 1970:1974) && any(neg_years %in% 2008:2012), "spread negative in the early 1970s and from 2008")
r30 <- s[fmid %/% 12L %in% 1930:1939, median(bp5 / bp1)]
chk(r30 > 2, "1930s: high-beta B/P more than twice low-beta B/P")
pct_end12 <- mean(sp_rep$spread <= end12)
chk(end12 < 0 && pct_end12 < 0.1, "December 2012 spread negative and in the lowest decile of 1968-2012")
```

@fig-spread shows the valuation cycle that defines GFKSW's states (their Figures 3 and 5). The spread is positive in `r p2(mean(sp_rep$spread > 0), 0)`% of the 540 formation months between December 1967 and November 2012, so high-beta stocks normally trade at a valuation premium. The spread was negative in the early 1970s and, from 2008 onwards, in most months of the following decade. Its largest reversal occurred during the Great Depression: in the median month of the 1930s, the average B/P ratio of high-beta stocks was `r f2(r30, 1)` times that of low-beta stocks (Appendix @fig-bp). At the end of December 2012, when GFKSW's sample ends, the spread stood at `r f2(end12)`, at the `r f2(100 * pct_end12, 0)`th percentile of the 540 formation months of their sample, and it has stayed below the upper two breakpoints since. The cheapest states for low-beta stocks occurred mainly in 1978--1981, 1988 and 1999--2000, the most expensive ones in 1970--1974 and 2005--2012.

```{r}
#| label: fig-spread
#| fig-cap: "B/P spread of the beta quintiles (average book-to-price ratio of the low-beta minus that of the high-beta quintile; stock-level B/P trimmed cross-sectionally at 0.5% in each tail), measured at the end of each formation month from December 1967 to November 2024. Dotted horizontal lines: breakpoints between the five valuation states, estimated over the GFKSW formation months (state 1 below the lowest line, state 5 above the highest). Dashed vertical lines: first and last formation month of the GFKSW sample (December 1967, November 2012). Shaded: NBER recessions. The B/P levels since 1929 are shown in @fig-bp."
#| fig-height: 2.5

x <- s[fmid >= ym(1967L, 12L) & mid <= cfg$full[2]][, date := eom(fmid)]
A_ <- A[order(state)]; brk <- (A_$to[1:4] + A_$from[2:5]) / 2
ylab_ <- c(brk[1] - 0.07, (brk[1:3] + brk[2:4]) / 2, brk[4] + 0.07)
ggplot(x, aes(date, spread)) +
  geom_rect(data = nber[start > as.Date("1968-01-01")], aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) + geom_hline(yintercept = brk, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.35, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(eom(ym(1967L, 12L)), eom(ym(2012L, 11L))), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey15") + labs(x = NULL, y = "B/P spread (Q1 - Q5)") + theme_paper +
  annotate("text", x = eom(ym(2025L, 6L)), y = ylab_, label = 1:5, size = 2.2, colour = "grey30", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = eom(ym(2025L, 6L)), y = brk[4] + 0.17, label = "state", size = 2.2, colour = "grey30", hjust = 0) +
  scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.06)))
```
