```{r}
#| label: tab-t2bc
mk <- function(stg) {
  z <- B[strategy == stg][order(state)]
  e <- as.data.frame(lapply(z[, c("12", "24", "36", "48", "60")], function(v) f2(100 * v)))
  tt <- B2[strategy == stg & h == 12][order(state)]
  tv <- VPW[strategy == stg & h == 12][order(state)]
  p <- as.data.frame(apply(gB[[stg]], 2, function(v) paste0("[", f2(v), "]")))
  cbind(State = states_lab, e, tt = f2(tt$t_boot), tv = f2(tv$t_ret), p[, c(1, 5)])
}
pB <- rbind(mk("LH"), mk("BN"))
names(pB) <- c("State", "12", "24", "36", "48", "60", "Baseline", "Vol.-pres.", "12", "60")
kbl(pB, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, linesep = "", align = "lrrrrrrrrr",
    caption = "Annualised future cumulative excess returns by initial B/P spread state, 1968--2012 (GFKSW Table 2, Panels B and C)",
    label = "t2bc") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 8) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Horizon (months)" = 5, "12 months" = 2, "Horizon" = 2), escape = FALSE) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "This replication (\\\\%)" = 5, "Bootstrap $t$" = 2, "GFKSW (\\\\%)" = 2), escape = FALSE) |>
  pack_rows("Panel A: low-minus-high (L--H)", 1, 5, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  pack_rows("Panel B: beta neutral (BN)", 6, 10, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = paste0("State cut-offs (B/P spread): ", paste(f2(A[order(state)]$to[1:4]), collapse = ", "), " (GFKSW: $-$0.01, 0.12, 0.22, 0.27; Appendix Table \\\\ref{tab:t2}). For every formation month, the strategy's monthly excess returns over the next $h$ ",
    "months are compounded and annualised; the table averages them by state. Windows end by December 2012. Bootstrap $t$: one-year mean divided by ",
    "the standard deviation of a circular block bootstrap of monthly returns (24-month blocks, ", res$boot_info$B, " draws) with the state calendar held fixed ",
    "(baseline) and of its volatility-preserving variant (Section 3.3); it tests whether the state average differs from zero. Published GFKSW values in brackets."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
```

Table \ref{tab:t2bc} reproduces GFKSW's pattern at the extremes. When low-beta stocks start cheapest (state 5), L--H earns `r p2(b12("LH", 5), 1)`% over the following year (GFKSW: 12.52%); when they start most expensive (state 1), `r p2(b12("LH", 1), 1)`% (GFKSW: $-5.80$%). The beta-neutral portfolio earns `r p2(b12("BN", 5), 1)`% after state 5 (GFKSW: 10.27%), but only `r p2(b12("BN", 1), 1)`% after state 1 (GFKSW: 2.30%), and unlike GFKSW's, its average return is negative at two and three years after state 2. The middle states do not replicate. Our state cut-offs lie above GFKSW's (`r paste(f2(A[order(state)]$to[1:4]), collapse = ", ")` against $-0.01$, 0.12, 0.22, 0.27), the next-month L--H return has the opposite sign in states 2 to 4 (Appendix Table \ref{tab:t2}), and the one-year returns in states 3 and 4 are `r p2(b12("LH", 3), 1)`% and `r p2(b12("LH", 4), 1)`% against $-6.84$% and $+3.36$%. Because the middle states span narrow ranges of the spread, their classification is fragile: with calendar-year instead of June-lagged book equity `r p2(1 - agree_fy, 0)`% of the months change state, with value-weighted instead of equal-weighted B/P averages `r p2(1 - agree_vw, 0)`%. Yet the one-year L--H returns of states 2 to 4 move by at most `r f2(100 * mid_shift, 1)` percentage points across these and three trimming variants, and no variant reproduces GFKSW's middle states (Appendix Table \ref{tab:a2}).

These estimates are imprecise. With the baseline bootstrap the one-year means are significant only in state 5 for L--H and in states 4 and 5 for BN, but this bootstrap over-rejects for the state-5 means when volatility follows its observed path, and with the volatility-preserving bootstrap the state-5 mean of L--H is not significant ($t$ = `r f2(VPW[strategy == "LH" & h == 12 & state == 5, t_ret])`); the bootstrap standard errors of the one-year L--H means are `r f2(min(se_lh), 1)` to `r f2(max(se_lh), 1)` percentage points. The contrast that carries GFKSW's argument, state 5 minus state 1, is `r f2(100 * d51("LH"), 1)` percentage points per year for L--H ($t$ = `r f2(d51("LH", "t_d_ret"))`, $p$ = `r pv(bc("LH", "null", 24L, "p_null"))`) and `r f2(100 * d51("BN"), 1)` points for BN ($t$ = `r f2(d51("BN", "t_d_ret"))`, $p$ = `r pv(bc("BN", "null", 24L, "p_null"))`). The cheap-minus-expensive contrasts are not robustly significant at the 5% level (Appendix Tables \ref{tab:inf} and \ref{tab:size}): across block lengths of 12 to 60 months the L--H $t$-statistic ranges from `r f2(t_rng("LH")[1])` to `r f2(t_rng("LH")[2])`; the volatility-preserving bootstrap gives `r f2(bc("LH", "vp", 24L, "t"))` (BN: `r f2(bc("BN", "vp", 24L, "t"))`); and under the observed volatility path a 5% test needs $|t|$ above `r f2(sct("LH", "observed_vol", "null24", "d51", "crit95"))` for L--H and `r f2(sct("BN", "observed_vol", "null24", "d51", "crit95"))` for BN. At three and five years the L--H contrast is `r f2(100 * d51("LH", "d_ret", 36), 1)` and `r f2(100 * d51("LH", "d_ret", 60), 1)` points per year and far from significant. The contrast also rests on one decade: state-5 months in `r paste(range(yrs5_2000), collapse = "--")` were followed by the collapse of the technology bubble (L--H: `r p2(lh_after(yrs5_2000, 5), 0)`% in the following year), state-1 months in 2008--2009 by the rebound of high-beta stocks (`r p2(lh_after(2008:2009, 1), 0)`%), and without the formation months of the 2000s the contrast falls to `r f2(100 * ld(2000L, "lh12"), 1)` points (Appendix Table \ref{tab:a6}).

A predictive regression avoids the classification step and tests a different hypothesis: a linear relation between the spread and the next-year return across all months, not a difference between the returns after the two extreme states. A one-standard-deviation higher spread predicts a `r p2(pr[sample == "rep" & strategy == "LH", slope], 1)` percentage points higher L--H return over the next 12 months ($t$ = `r f2(pr[sample == "rep" & strategy == "LH", t])`, Newey-West with 12 lags) and a `r p2(pr[sample == "rep" & strategy == "BN", slope], 1)` points higher BN return ($t$ = `r f2(pr[sample == "rep" & strategy == "BN", t])`). The spread is persistent (annual autocorrelation `r f2(ahv("rep", "LH", "ah_rho"))`) and its innovations are negatively correlated with the returns, so on the `r ahv("rep", "LH", "ah_n")` non-overlapping December observations we correct for the Stambaugh bias: the reduced-bias $t$-statistics are `r f2(ahv("rep", "LH", "ah_t"))` for L--H and `r f2(ahv("rep", "BN", "ah_t"))` for BN. Controlling for the market's excess return over the preceding year, which is positively correlated with the spread (`r f2(pr[sample == "rep" & strategy == "LH", cor_spread_mkt12])`), lowers the spread's Newey-West $t$-statistics only slightly, from `r f2(pr[sample == "rep" & strategy == "LH", t])` and `r f2(pr[sample == "rep" & strategy == "BN", t])` to `r f2(pr[sample == "rep" & strategy == "LH", ctrl_t])` and `r f2(pr[sample == "rep" & strategy == "BN", ctrl_t])`. In sample, the valuation signal therefore predicts the return of the beta-neutral portfolio significantly, whereas for the zero-cost portfolio it is not significant once the bias is corrected.

## Value and momentum exposures

```{r}
#| label: tab-t3
mk3 <- function(stg) {
  z <- W[strategy == stg & h %in% c(12, 60)][order(state, h)]
  e <- dcast(z, state ~ h, value.var = c("a_capm", "a_4f")); tb_ <- dcast(z, state ~ h, value.var = c("t_boot_capm", "t_boot_4f"))
  g <- gfk3[[stg]]
  est <- data.frame(c1 = f2(100 * e$a_capm_12), g1 = f2(g$capm[, "a12"]), c2 = f2(100 * e$a_capm_60), g2 = f2(g$capm[, "a60"]),
                    c3 = f2(100 * e$a_4f_12), g3 = f2(g$f4[, "a12"]), c4 = f2(100 * e$a_4f_60), g4 = f2(g$f4[, "a60"]))
  tst <- data.frame(c1 = f2(tb_$t_boot_capm_12), g1 = f2(g$capm[, "t12"]), c2 = f2(tb_$t_boot_capm_60), g2 = f2(g$capm[, "t60"]),
                    c3 = f2(tb_$t_boot_4f_12), g3 = f2(g$f4[, "t12"]), c4 = f2(tb_$t_boot_4f_60), g4 = f2(g$f4[, "t60"]))
  interleave(est, tst, states_lab)
}
t3 <- rbind(mk3("LH"), mk3("BN"))
hm <- function(stg) { z <- W[strategy == stg & h == 12][order(state)]; paste0(f2(z$b_hml), " / ", f2(z$b_mom)) }
t3$hm <- ""; t3$hm[seq(1, 10, 2)] <- hm("LH"); t3$hm[seq(11, 20, 2)] <- hm("BN")
names(t3) <- c("State", "Ours", "GFKSW", "Ours", "GFKSW", "Ours", "GFKSW", "Ours", "GFKSW", "HML / MOM")
kbl(t3, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, linesep = "", align = "lrrrrrrrrr",
    caption = "Conditional alphas by initial B/P spread state, 1968--2012 (GFKSW Table 3)", label = "t3") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 7.5) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "12 months" = 2, "60 months" = 2, "12 months" = 2, "60 months" = 2, "12 months" = 1)) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "CAPM alpha" = 4, "Four-factor alpha" = 4, "Loadings" = 1)) |>
  pack_rows("Panel A: low-minus-high (L--H)", 1, 10, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  pack_rows("Panel B: beta neutral (BN)", 11, 20, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = paste0("Alphas in percent per month. For every formation month the strategy's excess returns over the next 12 or 60 months are ",
    "regressed on the market or on MKT, SMB, HML and MOM, and the intercepts are averaged by state. In parentheses: for our estimates the bootstrap ",
    "t-statistic (as in Table \\\\ref{tab:t2bc}); for GFKSW their published Newey-West t-statistic. Our GFKSW-style statistics are in Appendix ",
    "Table \\\\ref{tab:gfkt}. HML / MOM: average four-factor loadings over 12-month windows."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
```

Table \ref{tab:t3} replicates GFKSW's attribution. In state 5 the L--H portfolio has a CAPM alpha of `r f2(100 * w_("LH", 5, 12, "a_capm"))`% per month over the following year against GFKSW's 1.04%, and its GFKSW-style $t$-statistic is `r f2(w_("LH", 5, 12, "t_gfk_capm"))` against their 5.11, so even our reading of their procedure does not reproduce their precision. Adding SMB, HML and MOM lowers the alpha to `r f2(100 * w_("LH", 5, 12, "a_4f"))`% (GFKSW: 0.40%), while the HML loading of L--H rises from `r f2(w_("LH", 1, 12, "b_hml"))` in state 1 to `r f2(w_("LH", 5, 12, "b_hml"))` in state 5 and the MOM loading from `r f2(w_("LH", 1, 12, "b_mom"))` to `r f2(w_("LH", 5, 12, "b_mom"))`, the pattern of GFKSW's Table 4 (Appendix Table \ref{tab:a3}; rolling correlations in Appendix @fig-cor). The loadings show a value exposure of the cheap-state premium, not a full explanation: when low-beta stocks are cheap relative to high-beta stocks, a portfolio long low-beta and short high-beta stocks is long value.

With the baseline bootstrap, no four-factor alpha is significant at any of the five horizons from 12 to 60 months (largest $|t|$ = `r f2(max(abs(W$t_boot_4f)))`), whereas the state-5 CAPM alphas are significant at every horizon for both portfolios with this bootstrap, which over-rejects here. The volatility-preserving bootstrap keeps them significant only at `r andlist(vp_sig_h("LH"))` months for L--H and `r andlist(vp_sig_h("BN"))` months for BN, not over the first year (L--H: $t$ = `r f2(vpw("LH", 5, 12, "t_capm"))`). The state-5 CAPM alpha of L--H also comes largely from windows that start in the 1980s: without them it falls from `r f2(100 * ld(NA, "a5_lh"))`% to `r f2(100 * ld(1980L, "a5_lh"))`% per month. With book equity from @davis2000, the 1930--2012 sample shows the same ordering of the extreme states at every horizon, but after the cheapest state L--H gains only in the first two years (Appendix Table \ref{tab:t5}).

# Post-sample performance and valuation timing

```{r}
#| label: tab-post
lab6 <- c(Q1 = "Low beta (Q1)", Q5 = "High beta (Q5)", LH = "Low -- high", BN = "Beta neutral (25\\%)", BNd = "Beta neutral (ex ante)", MKT = "Market")
mk6 <- function(per) {
  z <- pp[period == per][match(names(lab6), portfolio)]
  isM <- z$portfolio == "MKT"
  data.frame(P = unname(lab6), m = f2(100 * z$mean_ex, 1), t = f2(z$t_ex), sr = f2(z$sharpe), b = f2(z$beta),
             a1 = ifelse(isM, "--", f2(100 * z$a_capm, 1)), t1 = ifelse(isM, "", f2(z$t_capm)),
             a4 = ifelse(isM, "--", f2(100 * z$a_4f, 1)), t4 = ifelse(isM, "", f2(z$t_4f)))
}
df <- rbind(mk6("rep"), mk6("post"), mk6("pub"))
names(df) <- c("Portfolio", "Excess (\\%)", "$t$", "Sharpe", "Beta", "CAPM $\\alpha$ (\\%)", "$t$", "4F $\\alpha$ (\\%)", "$t$")
kbl(df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, linesep = "", align = "lrrrrrrrr",
    caption = "Performance in GFKSW's sample, after its end and after publication", label = "post") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 8) |>
  pack_rows("Panel A: GFKSW sample, 1968--2012 (540 months)", 1, 6, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  pack_rows("Panel B: after the original sample end, 2013--2024 (144 months)", 7, 12, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  pack_rows("Panel C: after publication, 2016--2024 (108 months)", 13, 18, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = paste0("Annualised mean excess returns, Sharpe ratios, realised market betas and annualised CAPM and four-factor alphas. ",
    "Newey-West t-statistics with $\\\\lfloor 4(T/100)^{2/9}\\\\rfloor$ lags (", nw_l(540), " in Panel A, ", nw_l(144), " in Panel B, ",
    nw_l(108), " in Panel C)."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
```

GFKSW's sample ends in December 2012 and their article appeared in mid-2015, so 2013--2024 lies after the original sample end, and only 2016--2024 after publication. Neither period is an untouched out-of-sample test for us, since the data existed before we specified anything. Classified with the 1968--2012 breakpoints, `r cnt("post", 1)` of the 144 post-sample formation months fall into state 1, `r cnt("post", 2)` into state 2, `r cnt("post", 3)` into state 3 and none into states 4 or 5 (after publication: `r cnt("pub", 1)`, `r cnt("pub", 2)` and `r cnt("pub", 3)`). The period therefore cannot test GFKSW's central prediction, that low-beta stocks win after starting cheap.

What it does show is mostly market beta (Table \ref{tab:post}). The annualised mean excess return of L--H over T-bills was `r p2(pf("post", "LH", "mean_ex"), 1)`% in 2013--2024 and `r p2(pf("pub", "LH", "mean_ex"), 1)`% in 2016--2024. In a CAPM decomposition for 2013--2024, its realised beta of `r f2(pf("post", "LH", "beta"))` times the market's mean excess return of `r p2(pf("post", "MKT", "mean_ex"), 1)`% gives `r p2(pf("post", "LH", "beta") * pf("post", "MKT", "mean_ex"), 1)`% per year, against a CAPM alpha of `r p2(pf("post", "LH", "a_capm"), 1)`% ($t$ = `r f2(pf("post", "LH", "t_capm"))`): the decomposition attributes the negative excess return mainly to the short market exposure in a rising market. Of the beta-neutral portfolio's mean excess return of `r p2(pf("post", "BN", "mean_ex"), 1)`% per year, the CAPM attributes `r p2(pf("post", "BN", "beta") * pf("post", "MKT", "mean_ex"), 1)` points to its beta of `r f2(pf("post", "BN", "beta"))`; the shrunk-beta version, with a realised beta of `r f2(pf("post", "BNs", "beta"))`, earned `r p2(pf("post", "BNs", "mean_ex"), 1)`% ($t$ = `r f2(pf("post", "BNs", "t_ex"))`, Appendix Table \ref{tab:ls}). The low-beta quintile had a lower Sharpe ratio than the market (`r f2(pf("post", "Q1", "sharpe"))` against `r f2(pf("post", "MKT", "sharpe"))`) but a positive CAPM alpha of `r p2(pf("post", "Q1", "a_capm"), 1)`% per year ($t$ = `r f2(pf("post", "Q1", "t_capm"))`); twelve years cannot distinguish a premium of the 1968--2012 size (`r p2(pf("rep", "Q1", "a_capm"), 1)`% per year) from zero. With only `r ahv("post", "LH", "ah_n")` non-overlapping years, the predictive regression after 2012 has little power: the reduced-bias L--H slope is of similar size as before (`r p2(ahv("post", "LH", "ah_b"), 1)` against `r p2(ahv("rep", "LH", "ah_b"), 1)` percentage points per standard deviation, $t$ = `r f2(ahv("post", "LH", "ah_t"))`), whereas the BN slope turns negative ($t$ = `r f2(ahv("post", "BN", "ah_t"))`).

Can the valuation signal be used in real time? With breakpoints estimated only from earlier months, the one-year L--H return after a real-time state-5 signal is `r p2(res$T2_rt[strategy == "LH" & state == 5 & h == 12, value], 1)`% and after a state-1 signal `r p2(res$T2_rt[strategy == "LH" & state == 1 & h == 12, value], 1)`%. GFKSW explicitly do not propose a timing rule; Table \ref{tab:timing} tests the simplest one their results suggest: hold the long-short portfolio only when the real-time state is 4 or 5, in a second variant only if the strategy's own trailing 12-month return is also positive (time-series momentum of the strategy, not the MOM factor). For L--H, timing turns a negative net Sharpe ratio into a small positive one, mainly by avoiding the short market exposure, but not significantly (Holm $p$ = `r pv(tmr("full", "LH", "val", "p_holm"))`); for the beta-neutral portfolio it lowers the net Sharpe ratio from `r f2(tmr("full", "BN", "always", "sharpe_net"))` to `r f2(tmr("full", "BN", "val", "sharpe_net"))`. After 2012 the real-time states never exceeded 3, so the rule held T-bills throughout. The tested rules bring no statistically significant net Sharpe ratio improvement, which does not prove that timing is useless; timing factors with their own valuation spreads is known to be hard [@asness2017].

```{r}
#| label: tab-timing
lab7 <- c(always = "Always invested", val = "Valuation (states 4--5)", vm = "Valuation and own momentum")
mk7 <- function(stg) {
  z <- tm[period == "full" & strategy == stg][match(names(lab7), rule)]
  est <- data.frame(inv = f2(100 * z$invested, 0), m = f2(100 * z$mean_ex, 1), sr = f2(z$sharpe), a1 = f2(100 * z$a_capm, 1),
                    a4 = f2(100 * z$a_4f, 1), srn = f2(z$sharpe_net), d = ifelse(is.na(z$sr_diff), "--", f2(z$sr_diff)),
                    ph = ifelse(is.na(z$p_holm), "--", pv(z$p_holm)))
  tst <- data.frame(inv = "", m = f2(z$t_ex), sr = "", a1 = f2(z$t_capm), a4 = f2(z$t_4f), srn = "",
                    d = ifelse(is.na(z$sr_se), "", f2(z$sr_se)), ph = "")
  interleave(est, tst, unname(lab7))
}
df <- rbind(mk7("LH"), mk7("BN"))
names(df) <- c("Rule", "Invested (\\%)", "Excess (\\%)", "SR", "CAPM $\\alpha$ (\\%)", "4F $\\alpha$ (\\%)", "SR net", "$\\Delta$SR net", "Holm $p$")
kbl(df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, linesep = "", align = "lrrrrrrrr",
    caption = paste0("Real-time valuation timing of the long-short portfolios, ", res$rt_start %/% 12, "--2024 (exploratory)"), label = "timing") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"), font_size = 7.5) |>
  pack_rows("Low-minus-high (L--H)", 1, 6, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  pack_rows("Beta neutral (BN)", 7, 12, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = paste0("States are classified each month with quintile breakpoints from earlier formation months only (expanding window, at least ",
    "ten years from 1968). The portfolio is held when the real-time state is 4 or 5 (valuation), additionally only when its own trailing 12-month ",
    "return is positive (valuation and own momentum), and otherwise T-bills are held. Annualised; in parentheses Newey-West t-statistics and, for ",
    "$\\\\Delta$SR net, the Ledoit-Wolf standard error. SR net deducts 10 bp per dollar traded, the lending fee and the cost of switching in and out. ",
    "$\\\\Delta$SR net: difference to the always-invested net Sharpe ratio; Holm-adjusted p-values over the four comparisons."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
```

# Beta forecasts and portfolio performance

GFKSW sort on betas from 60 monthly returns. Daily returns contain more information about co-movement but are noisier and suffer from non-synchronous trading [@dimson1979; @hollstein2019]. Appendix Table \ref{tab:beta} compares seven estimators, which differ in return frequency and window. Holding the window at 36 months, daily returns forecast the realised beta of the same portfolios significantly better than monthly returns (Diebold-Mariano $t$ = `r f2(dmv("beta_D36", "beta_M36", "dm_t"))`). Holding the frequency fixed, short windows are worse: the 36-month monthly beta is less accurate than the 60-month one ($t$ = `r f2(dmv("beta_M36", "beta_M60", "dm_t"))`), and the three-month daily beta less accurate than the 36-month one ($t$ = `r f2(dmv("beta_D3", "beta_D36", "dm_t"))`). Against GFKSW's 60-month monthly beta, only the 36-month daily beta and the Dimson-corrected 12-month daily beta have significantly smaller squared errors (Holm $p$ = `r pv(dmv("beta_D36", "beta_M60", "p_holm"))` and `r pv(dmv("beta_DD12", "beta_M60", "p_holm"))`), and these results survive a Holm adjustment over all ten forecast comparisons (largest adjusted $p$ = `r pv(max(dm_key$p_holm_all))`). Daily betas are thus better risk forecasts when the window is long enough, in line with @hollstein2019.

As strategies, the estimated ranking reverses. The ex-ante beta-neutral portfolio formed on the 60-month monthly beta has the highest gross Sharpe ratio (`r f2(xA[spec == "beta_M60", bnd_sharpe])`); every daily specification has a lower one (`r f2(min(xA[grepl("beta_D", spec), bnd_sharpe]))` to `r f2(max(xA[grepl("beta_D", spec), bnd_sharpe]))`), but no difference in gross Sharpe ratios is significant after the Holm adjustment (smallest adjusted $p$ = `r pv(min(srb$p_holm))`). The valuation effect is also largest with the 60-month monthly beta. A plausible but untested explanation is that slow-moving monthly betas capture persistent firm characteristics such as value and leverage, whereas daily betas measure current co-movement. The daily-beta portfolio of Section 7 uses the 12-month daily beta, which is not among the significantly better forecasters; we do not switch to the best forecaster after the fact.

# Long-only implementation after trading costs

Where does the premium come from? In 1968--2012 the high-beta quintile's CAPM alpha was `r p2(pf("rep", "Q5", "a_capm"), 1)`% per year ($t$ = `r f2(pf("rep", "Q5", "t_capm"))`) and the low-beta quintile's `r p2(pf("rep", "Q1", "a_capm"), 1)`% ($t$ = `r f2(pf("rep", "Q1", "t_capm"))`, Table \ref{tab:post}): `r p2(short_share, 0)`% of the L--H alpha comes from the short side. Most investors cannot or will not short and are judged against a cap-weighted benchmark [@baker2011; @blitz2014]; for them the question is whether a long-only low-beta portfolio beats the portfolio they would otherwise hold. All portfolios in Table \ref{tab:lo} are formed from the same large-cap universe over 1968--2024, rebalanced at month ends and charged costs on their own turnover: the value-weighted low-beta quintile; a buffer rule that buys stocks entering the lowest 20% of betas and sells them only when they leave the lowest 30%; quarterly rebalancing; the quintile with target weights capped at 5% per stock at each rebalancing; the quintile formed on 12-month daily betas; and two long-only global minimum-variance portfolios with a 3% weight cap, one estimated with the constant-correlation shrinkage of @ledoit2004 on 60 monthly returns, the other with the nonlinear shrinkage of @ledoit2020 on the daily returns of the last 12 months. With on average `r f2(res$minvar_info[, mean(n)], 0)` (monthly) and `r f2(res$minvar_nl_info[, mean(n)], 0)` (daily) eligible stocks, the sample covariance matrix is singular in both cases. The benchmarks are the cap-weighted portfolio of the same universe and the equally weighted $1/N$ portfolio [@demiguel2009].

```{r}
#| label: tab-lo
ord <- c("LowBeta", "LowBeta buffer", "LowBeta quarterly", "LowBeta capped", "LowBeta (daily 12m)", "Min-variance", "Min-variance NL", "Large-cap EW", "Large-cap VW")
hdr <- c("Q1", "Buffer", "Quarterly", "Capped", "Daily $\\beta$", "Monthly", "Daily", "$1/N$", "Cap-wt.")
g <- LO[match(ord, strategy)]; n <- LOn[match(ord, strategy)]; b <- BE[match(ord, strategy)]; v <- dv[match(ord, strategy)]
isB <- ord == "Large-cap VW"
na_ <- function(x, cond) ifelse(cond, "--", x)
tr <- function(x, cond = FALSE, l = "(", r = ")") ifelse(rep_len(cond, length(x)), "", paste0(l, x, r))   # t-statistic / standard error row
rw <- function(lab, v) as.data.frame(t(c(lab, v)), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
df <- rbind(
  rw("Excess return (\\%)", f2(100 * g$mean_ex, 1)), rw("Volatility (\\%)", f2(100 * g$vol, 1)),
  rw("Sharpe ratio", f2(g$sharpe)), rw("Max. drawdown (\\%)", f2(100 * g$mdd, 0)), rw("Market beta", f2(g$beta)),
  rw("CAPM $\\alpha$ (\\%)", f2(100 * g$alpha_capm, 1)), rw("", tr(f2(g$t_capm))),
  rw("Four-factor $\\alpha$ (\\%)", f2(100 * g$alpha_4f, 1)), rw("", tr(f2(g$t_4f))), rw("HML loading", f2(g$b_hml)),
  rw("Active return (\\%)", na_(f2(100 * g$active, 1), isB)), rw("", tr(f2(g$t_active), isB)),
  rw("Tracking error (\\%)", na_(f2(100 * g$te, 1), isB)), rw("Information ratio", na_(f2(g$active / g$te), isB)),
  rw("Turnover (\\% p.a.)", f2(100 * g$to, 0)), rw("Sharpe ratio, net", f2(n$sharpe)),
  rw("$\\Delta$SR net", na_(f2(n$sr_diff), isB)), rw("", tr(f2(n$sr_se), isB, "[", "]")),
  rw("$p$-value", ifelse(isB, "--", pv(n$p_sr))), rw("Holm $p$-value", ifelse(isB, "--", pv(n$p_holm))),
  rw("Break-even cost (bp)", ifelse(is.finite(b$be_sr), f2(b$be_sr, 0), ifelse(isB, "--", "<0"))),
  rw("Positions", f2(v$n, 0)), rw("Largest weight (\\%)", f2(100 * v$wmax, 1)), rw("Effective N", f2(v$effn, 0)))
names(df) <- c("", hdr)
kbl(df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, linesep = "", align = "lrrrrrrrrr",
    caption = "Long-only low-beta and minimum-variance portfolios versus the cap-weighted benchmark, 1968--2024", label = "lo") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"), font_size = 8) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Low-beta quintile" = 5, "Minimum variance" = 2, "Benchmarks" = 2)) |>
  pack_rows("Panel A: gross performance", 1, 14, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  pack_rows("Panel B: costs (scenario: 10 bp per dollar traded)", 15, 21, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  pack_rows("Panel C: diversification (averages over rebalancing dates)", 22, 24, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = paste0("Annualised; Newey-West t-statistics (", nw_l(684), " lags) in parentheses, standard errors in brackets. Capped: quintile weights capped at 5\\\\%; Daily $\\\\beta$: quintile ",
    "formed on 12-month daily betas; minimum variance with a 3\\\\% cap, covariance matrix from 60 monthly returns (constant-correlation shrinkage) or from ",
    "the daily returns of the last 12 months (nonlinear shrinkage). Cap-wt.: value-weighted portfolio of all universe stocks (benchmark of the tests); the ",
    "Fama-French market has an excess return of ", f2(100 * row_of(LO, "Market (FF)")$mean_ex, 1), "\\\\% and a Sharpe ratio of ", f2(row_of(LO, "Market (FF)")$sharpe), ". ",
    "Turnover: purchases plus sales relative to drifted weights. $\\\\Delta$SR net: Ledoit-Wolf (2008) HAC test against the cost-bearing benchmark; ",
    "the low-beta quintile is the primary comparison (unadjusted $p$), Holm adjustment over the ", length(n$p_holm[!is.na(n$p_holm)]), " candidates. Break-even: ",
    "one-way cost at which the net Sharpe ratio equals the benchmark's (values above 50 bp extrapolate beyond the highest cost scenario). Effective N: ",
    "$1/\\\\sum w_i^2$. Liquidity: Appendix Table \\\\ref{tab:liq}."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
```

The low-beta quintile delivers lower risk: `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$vol, 1)`% volatility, a beta of `r f2(row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$beta)` and a maximum drawdown of `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$mdd, 0)`%, against `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$vol, 1)`%, `r f2(row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$beta)` and `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$mdd, 0)`% for the benchmark, at a lower excess return (`r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$mean_ex, 1)`% against `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$mean_ex, 1)`% per year). Its Sharpe ratio is `r f2(row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$sharpe)` against `r f2(row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$sharpe)` gross and `r f2(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta")$sharpe)` against `r f2(row_of(LOn, "Large-cap VW")$sharpe)` after the base-case cost. This primary comparison is inconclusive: the difference of `r f2(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta")$sr_diff)` has a standard error of `r f2(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta")$sr_se)` ($p$ = `r pv(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta")$p_sr)`), consistent both with no advantage and with a sizeable one. Judged as an active manager, the portfolio trails the benchmark by `r f2(-100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$active, 1)`% per year with a tracking error of `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$te, 1)`% (information ratio `r f2(row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$active / row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$te)`): exactly the profile that makes benchmarked managers avoid low-beta stocks [@baker2011]. Its CAPM alpha of `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$alpha_capm, 1)`% per year ($t$ = `r f2(row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$t_capm)`) shrinks to `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$alpha_4f, 1)`% with the four-factor model (95% interval `r f2(100 * a4ci[1], 1)`% to `r f2(100 * a4ci[2], 1)`%), alongside an HML loading of `r f2(row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$b_hml)`.

The low-beta quintile turns over `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$to, 0)`% of its value per year, against `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$to, 0)`% for the benchmark, and its net Sharpe ratio would equal the benchmark's at a one-way cost of `r f2(row_of(BE, "LowBeta")$be_sr, 0)` basis points (Appendix @fig-costs). The buffer rule cuts turnover to `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta buffer")$to, 0)`% and raises the break-even cost to `r f2(row_of(BE, "LowBeta buffer")$be_sr, 0)` basis points, an extrapolation beyond the tested range of 0 to 50 basis points. In sample, the 5% cap raises the effective number of positions from `r f2(row_of(dv, "LowBeta")$effn, 0)` to `r f2(row_of(dv, "LowBeta capped")$effn, 0)` and turnover from `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$to, 0)`% to `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta capped")$to, 0)`%. Under the assumed cost model, the estimated net Sharpe ratio rises from `r f2(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta")$sharpe)` to `r f2(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta capped")$sharpe)`. These are descriptive results. The daily nonlinear-shrinkage implementation has the lowest realized volatility among the portfolios considered (`r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "Min-variance NL")$vol, 1)`%). Since return frequency, estimation window, estimator and stock selection differ at the same time from the monthly version, this is no isolated evidence that the estimator is superior. Its weights change so quickly that it turns over `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "Min-variance NL")$to, 0)`% per year and its net Sharpe ratio falls to `r f2(row_of(LOn, "Min-variance NL")$sharpe)` (break-even `r f2(row_of(BE, "Min-variance NL")$be_sr, 0)` basis points). The monthly version has the largest CAPM alpha (`r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "Min-variance")$alpha_capm, 1)`%, $t$ = `r f2(row_of(LO, "Min-variance")$t_capm)`) and the highest net Sharpe ratio (`r f2(row_of(LOn, "Min-variance")$sharpe, 3)`), closely followed by the buffer rule (`r f2(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta buffer")$sharpe, 3)`) and the capped quintile (`r f2(row_of(LOn, "LowBeta capped")$sharpe, 3)`). No net Sharpe ratio of the `r sum(!is.na(LOn$p_holm))` candidates differs significantly from the benchmark's after the Holm adjustment, and since 2013 every one of them has had a lower net Sharpe ratio than the benchmark (low-beta quintile: `r f2(row_of(LOp, "LowBeta")$sharpe)` against `r f2(row_of(LOp, "Large-cap VW")$sharpe)`).

The low-beta quintile is also concentrated: its largest position averages `r f2(100 * row_of(dv, "LowBeta")$wmax, 1)`% of the portfolio and its effective number of stocks is `r f2(row_of(dv, "LowBeta")$effn, 0)` against `r f2(row_of(dv, "Large-cap VW")$effn, 0)` for the benchmark. Its holdings rank like the benchmark's by dollar volume (Appendix Table \ref{tab:liq}). Proportional costs are modelled as scenarios, but actual execution costs and capacity, which depend on trade size and market impact, are not estimated. For investors who can short (Appendix Table \ref{tab:ls}), the beta-neutral portfolio keeps a net Sharpe ratio of `r f2(LS[strategy == "Beta neutral (fixed 25%)", sharpe_n])` over 1968--2024, the nearly beta-neutral version with shrunk betas only `r f2(LS[strategy == "Beta neutral (shrunk beta)", sharpe_n])`, and L--H a negative one despite a gross CAPM alpha with $t$ = `r f2(LS[strategy == "Low - high", t1_g])`; no long-short four-factor alpha is significant before or after costs.

# Risk measurement and performance across holding periods

Month-end data hide intra-month risk, and a strategy is experienced through the windows over which investors judge it, typically three to five years. We rebuild every portfolio's daily return path from CRSP's daily file with unchanged holdings, monthly rebalancing and weights drifting within the month; long-short positions are also reset only at month ends, and all returns are gross of costs. Every stock-month of the cap-weighted universe portfolio compounds to its monthly return except `r rcn("next_month_delisting") + rcn("conflict")` delisting months of `r format(sum(RCv$stock_months), big.mark = ",")`; their treatment changes the volatilities in Table \ref{tab:freq} by at most `r cl(100 * max(dmx$d_vol), 2)` percentage points and the Sharpe ratios by at most `r cl(max(dmx$d_sr), 3)` (other statistics: Appendix Table \ref{tab:daily}), so the comparison isolates the measurement frequency.

```{r}
#| label: tab-freq
ordf <- c("LowBeta", "HighBeta", "Min-variance", "Large-cap VW", "Beta neutral (fixed 25%)", "Low - high", "Market (FF)")
frx <- fr[match(ordf, strategy)]; fbx <- fb[match(ordf, strategy)]
df <- data.frame(P = c("Low beta (Q1)", "High beta (Q5)", "Min. variance (monthly)", "Cap weight", "Beta neutral (25\\%)", "Low -- high", "Market"),
  vd = f2(100 * frx$vol_daily, 1), vm = f2(100 * frx$vol_monthly, 1), sd = f2(frx$sharpe_daily), sm = f2(frx$sharpe_monthly),
  md = f2(100 * frx$mdd_daily, 0), mm = f2(100 * frx$mdd_monthly, 0), kd = f2(frx$kurt_daily, 1), km = f2(frx$kurt_monthly, 1),
  bd = f2(fbx$beta_daily), bm = f2(fbx$beta_monthly))
names(df) <- c("Portfolio", "Daily", "Monthly", "Daily", "Monthly", "Daily", "Monthly", "Daily", "Monthly", "Daily", "Monthly")
tab(df, "The same portfolios measured with daily and with monthly returns, 1968--2024", "freq",
    notes = paste0("Volatility and Sharpe ratios are annualised with 252 days or 12 months; drawdowns, kurtosis and betas are not. Monthly returns compound the daily returns ",
      "of the same holdings, so rebalancing is monthly in both cases. Kurtosis: excess kurtosis of daily or monthly excess returns, i.e. different horizons. Beta: slope on the market excess ",
      "return at each frequency. Gross returns; daily paths from CRSP's daily file (dsf\\\\_v2); excess returns over the ",
      "T-bill return compounded from daily rates. Long-short portfolios: total returns, legs reset at month ends."),
    align = "lrrrrrrrrrr", fs = 7.5, wide = TRUE,
    header = c(" " = 1, "Volatility (%)" = 2, "Sharpe ratio" = 2, "Max. drawdown (%)" = 2, "Excess kurtosis" = 2, "Market beta" = 2))
```

Table \ref{tab:freq} shows that frequency matters for risk measurement more than for the ranking. Annualised daily volatility exceeds monthly volatility for the low-beta quintile (`r f2(100 * fr[strategy == "LowBeta", vol_daily], 1)`% versus `r f2(100 * fr[strategy == "LowBeta", vol_monthly], 1)`%) and the cap-weighted benchmark (`r f2(100 * fr[strategy == "Large-cap VW", vol_daily], 1)`% versus `r f2(100 * fr[strategy == "Large-cap VW", vol_monthly], 1)`%), but not for the minimum-variance portfolio. With serially uncorrelated daily returns the two would agree up to sampling error and compounding effects. The variance ratio of overlapping 21-day to daily log returns [@lo1988], which differs from the squared ratio of the volatilities in the table because it uses log returns and overlapping windows rather than calendar months, is `r f2(vrt[strategy == "LowBeta", vr], 3)` for the low-beta quintile and `r f2(vrt[strategy == "Large-cap VW", vr], 3)` for the benchmark, with heteroskedasticity-robust $z$-statistics of `r f2(vrt[strategy == "LowBeta", z])` and `r f2(vrt[strategy == "Large-cap VW", z])`: the gap is consistent with mild negative serial correlation within the month, but the data do not establish it. Daily drawdowns are at least as deep, because intra-month troughs are invisible in month-end data, and daily returns are far more fat-tailed. The low-beta quintile's beta is higher with daily data (`r f2(fb[strategy == "LowBeta", beta_daily])` versus `r f2(fb[strategy == "LowBeta", beta_monthly])`), and the beta-neutral portfolio's daily beta of `r f2(fb[strategy == "Beta neutral (fixed 25%)", beta_daily])` (Newey-West standard error `r f2(fb[strategy == "Beta neutral (fixed 25%)", se_daily])`) confirms that it carries market risk at both frequencies. Sharpe ratios change by at most `r f2(max(abs(fr$sharpe_daily - fr$sharpe_monthly)), 2)` between frequencies. The monthly columns differ slightly from Table \ref{tab:lo} only through the T-bill return compounded from daily rates (up to `r f2(1e4 * max(t78$max_rf_diff), 0)` basis points per month away from the monthly series) and, for the market, compound the daily Fama-French factor; with the monthly T-bill series the Sharpe ratios of Table \ref{tab:lo} are reproduced exactly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-roll
#| fig-cap: "Rolling 36- and 60-month evaluation windows of monthly gross returns, plotted at the window's last month; the first windows end in December 1970 (36 months) and December 1972 (60 months), the last in December 2024. Top: annualised Sharpe ratio (from excess returns) of the low-beta quintile and of the minimum-variance portfolio (monthly estimation) minus that of the cap-weighted benchmark of the same universe. Middle: CAPM alpha of the low-beta quintile and of the minimum-variance portfolio (monthly estimation), in percent per year. Bottom: annualised volatility, in percent, of the low-beta quintile, the minimum-variance portfolio and the cap-weighted benchmark."
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-width: 7
r <- copy(roll)[, date := eom(mid)]
d1 <- melt(r[, .(date, window, "Low beta (Q1)" = sr_lb - sr_vw, "Minimum variance" = sr_mv - sr_vw)],
           id.vars = c("date", "window"))[, panel := "SR diff."]
d2 <- melt(r[, .(date, window, "Low beta (Q1)" = 100 * a_lb, "Minimum variance" = 100 * a_mv)], id.vars = c("date", "window"))[, panel := "Alpha (%)"]
d3 <- melt(r[, .(date, window, "Low beta (Q1)" = 100 * vol_lb, "Minimum variance" = 100 * vol_mv, "Cap weight" = 100 * vol_vw)],
           id.vars = c("date", "window"))[, panel := "Vol. (%)"]
d <- rbind(d1, d2, d3)
d[, variable := factor(variable, levels = c("Low beta (Q1)", "Minimum variance", "Cap weight"))]
d[, window := paste0(window, "-month window")]
d[, panel := factor(panel, levels = c("SR diff.", "Alpha (%)", "Vol. (%)"))]
hl <- data.table(panel = factor(c("SR diff.", "Alpha (%)"), levels = levels(d$panel)), y = 0)
ggplot(d, aes(date, value, colour = variable, linetype = variable)) + geom_hline(data = hl, aes(yintercept = y), linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ window, scales = "free_y") + scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[1], col_mv, pal[5])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid", "dashed")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_paper + theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1), linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 1))
```

Rolling evaluation windows (@fig-roll), distinct from the fixed 60-month estimation windows of betas and covariances, show what an investor would have experienced. The risk reduction is the most stable property of the low-beta quintile: its volatility is below the benchmark's in `r p2(rs[window == 36, vol], 0)`% of 36-month and `r p2(rs[window == 60, vol], 0)`% of 60-month windows, at `r f2(rs[window == 36, vr_min], 2)` to `r f2(rs[window == 36, vr_max], 2)` times the benchmark's volatility over 36 months. Its return advantage is not: it has a higher Sharpe ratio than the benchmark in `r p2(rs[window == 36, sr], 0)`% of 36-month and `r p2(rs[window == 60, sr], 0)`% of 60-month windows, a positive CAPM alpha in `r p2(rs[window == 60, a], 0)`% of 60-month windows, and a higher raw return than the benchmark in only `r p2(rs[window == 60, act], 0)`% of 60-month windows. The minimum-variance portfolio has the higher Sharpe ratio in `r p2(rs[window == 60, mv], 0)`% of 60-month windows. Overlapping windows are strongly dependent, so these shares describe experience, not independent evidence. The pattern is consistent with the benchmarking explanation of why the anomaly persists [@baker2011]: a strategy that trails its benchmark for years is hard to hold, even when its risk-adjusted return is higher over the full sample.

\FloatBarrier

# Conclusion

GFKSW's unconditional results replicate almost exactly. The one-year conditional L--H returns also reproduce the pattern at the extremes: positive after the cheapest state and negative after the most expensive state. The middle states do not replicate, and, in our reconstruction and simulations, Newey-West statistics of averages over overlapping windows overstate precision. The cheap-minus-expensive contrasts are not robustly significant at the 5% level. That of the zero-cost portfolio rests largely on the technology bust and the 2009 rebound. A bias-corrected predictive regression, which tests a different hypothesis, shows in sample that valuation predicts the beta-neutral portfolio's return, but the conditional premium coincides largely with a value exposure, no four-factor alpha is significant with the block bootstraps or calendar-time regressions, and the tested timing rules did not significantly improve the net Sharpe ratio. Since 2013 valuations have never been cheap enough to test GFKSW's central prediction, and a CAPM decomposition attributes the zero-cost portfolio's negative excess returns mainly to its negative beta in a rising market.

For long-only investors, an implementation gap remains: about two thirds of the L--H portfolio's CAPM alpha in 1968--2012 comes from shorting high-beta stocks. The most stable result is the historical risk reduction. A long-only low-beta portfolio cut volatility by about a fifth and the maximum drawdown from `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "Large-cap VW")$mdd, 0)`% to `r f2(100 * row_of(LO, "LowBeta")$mdd, 0)`%, but neither a net Sharpe ratio advantage over the benchmark nor a timing advantage is established, and investors must accept deep drawdowns and long benchmark underperformance. In the variants studied, the buffer rule reduces turnover and the weight cap concentration, without proven general superiority. Better risk forecasts from daily betas did not yield significantly higher gross Sharpe ratios, and the daily nonlinear-shrinkage portfolio has the lowest realized volatility but no higher net Sharpe ratio than the low-beta quintile.

Four limitations remain: the valuation states rest on few episodes, so test sizes depend on how their volatility is modelled; CRSP data vintages differ from GFKSW's; the proportional cost model uses scenario values and ignores market impact, financing spreads and borrowing constraints; and the analysis is limited to US large caps.

mk5 <- function(stg) {
  z <- CT[strategy == stg][order(state, h)]
  e <- dcast(z, state ~ h, value.var = c("a_capm", "a_4f")); tt <- dcast(z, state ~ h, value.var = c("t_capm", "t_4f"))
  ee <- as.data.frame(lapply(e[, -1], function(v) f2(100 * v))); t2 <- as.data.frame(lapply(tt[, -1], f2))
  names(ee) <- names(t2) <- paste0("c", 1:6)
  interleave(ee, t2, states_lab)
}
t5x <- rbind(mk5("LH"), mk5("BN"))

    caption = "Alternative estimator: calendar-time regressions on stacked windows, 1968--2012", label = "a5") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 7.5) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "CAPM alpha" = 3, "Four-factor alpha" = 3)) |>

  footnote(general = paste0("Alphas in percent per month. All window-month observations of a state are stacked and estimated in one regression, which ",
    "equals a weighted regression on calendar months with weights equal to the number of windows covering each month. The estimand is a ",
    "window-weighted average of monthly abnormal returns with factor loadings common to all windows of the state, not the average of window ",
    "alphas in Table \\\\ref{tab:t3}. Newey-West t-statistics (12 lags) in parentheses, computed on the full monthly calendar: months that no window ",
    "covers enter with a zero score, so that each lag spans calendar months."), general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)

```{r}
#| label: tab-size
tests <- c(gfksw_nw = "GFKSW-style Newey-West", null24 = "Null model, 24-month blocks", null60 = "Null model, 60-month blocks",
           vp24 = "Volatility-preserving, 24-month blocks", pairs24 = "Formation-month blocks, 24 months")
mk_sz <- function(stg) {
  r_ <- function(tst, st, g) { x <- sct(stg, g, tst, st, "rej"); if (length(x)) f2(100 * x, 1) else "--" }
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(tests), function(tst) data.frame(T = tests[[tst]],
    a = r_(tst, "state5", "iid"), b = r_(tst, "state5", "garch"), c = r_(tst, "state5", "observed_vol"),
    d = r_(tst, "d51", "iid"), e = r_(tst, "d51", "garch"), f = r_(tst, "d51", "observed_vol"),
    g = { x <- sct(stg, "observed_vol", tst, "d51", "crit95"); if (length(x)) f2(x) else "--" })))
}
df <- rbind(mk_sz("LH"), mk_sz("BN"))
names(df) <- c("Test", "iid", "GARCH", "Obs. vol.", "iid", "GARCH", "Obs. vol.", "Obs. vol.")
kbl(df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, linesep = "", align = "lrrrrrrr",
    caption = "Simulated size of the tests for state averages and for the central contrast, one-year windows", label = "size") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 7.5) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "State-5 mean: rejections (\\\\%)" = 3, "State 5 $-$ state 1: rejections (\\\\%)" = 3, "Critical value" = 1), escape = FALSE) |>
  pack_rows("Low-minus-high (L--H)", 1, 5, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  pack_rows("Beta neutral (BN)", 6, 10, bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = paste0("Rejection rates of two-sided 5\\\\% tests of a true null (the states carry no information) in ", SCt$nsim[1], " simulated samples ",
    "of 540 months with the actual state calendar of 1968--2012, ", SCt$B[1], " bootstrap draws per sample. iid: normal returns with the strategy's mean ",
    "and volatility; GARCH: AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) with Student-$t$ errors, fitted to the strategy by maximum likelihood; Obs. vol.: the fitted AR(1) process with ",
    "Student-$t$ errors scaled by the fitted conditional volatility of the actual data, so that volatile periods stay where they occurred. Rejections are ",
    "counted around the simulated mean of each estimator. Critical value: 95\\\\% quantile of $|t|$ for the contrast under Obs. vol. (size-adjusted 5\\\\% ",
    "critical value). Monte Carlo standard errors of the rejection rates: at most ", f2(100 * max(SCt$mc_se), 1), " percentage points."),
    general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)

  footnote(general = paste0("Annualised percentages; Newey-West t-statistics in parentheses; Beta: realised market beta. Net returns deduct 10 bp per dollar ",
    "traded on both legs and a lending fee of 25 bp per year on the short notional (scenario values); the ex-ante and shrunk-beta versions also pay for ",
    "changes in the short ratio. Shrunk beta: short ratio $(0.6\\\\hat\\\\beta_{Q1}+0.4)/(0.6\\\\hat\\\\beta_{Q5}+0.4)$ as in Frazzini and Pedersen (2014). TO: annual ",
    "turnover of both legs in percent of capital."), general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-costs
#| fig-cap: "Net Sharpe ratio as a function of the one-way trading cost per dollar traded, 1968--2024, monthly rebalancing (buffer rule as described in Section 7). Costs are charged on each portfolio's turnover, including the cap-weighted benchmark's. All cost levels are scenarios, not estimates of actual costs; break-even costs above 50 basis points quoted in the text extrapolate beyond the range shown."
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| fig-width: 6.5
cc <- res$LO_costs[strategy %in% c("LowBeta", "LowBeta buffer", "Min-variance", "Large-cap VW", "Large-cap EW")]
cc[, strategy := factor(strategy, levels = c("LowBeta", "LowBeta buffer", "Min-variance", "Large-cap VW", "Large-cap EW"),
                        labels = c("Low beta (Q1)", "Low beta, buffer", "Minimum variance (monthly estimation)", "Cap weight (benchmark)", "Equal weight"))]
ggplot(cc, aes(1e4 * cost, sharpe, colour = strategy, linetype = strategy)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[1], col_buf, col_mv, pal[5], col_ew)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid", "solid", "dashed", "solid")) +
  labs(x = "One-way cost per dollar traded (basis points)", y = "Net Sharpe ratio") + theme_paper +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1), linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 1))
```

\FloatBarrier

## C. Reproducibility and use of AI tools {.unnumbered}

All results are produced by build.R, which reads the university database read-only (`r paste0("\\texttt{", gsub("_", "\\\\_\\\\allowbreak{}", basename(res$meta$db)), "}")`, `r f2(res$meta$db_size / 2^30, 1)` GB, last modified `r format(res$meta$db_mtime, "%d %B %Y")`), builds the stock panel, estimates all betas, forms all portfolios and stores every table and time series in results/res.rds; paper.qmd reads only results/res.rds. 

**Use of AI tools.** We used an AI assistant (Anthropic's Claude) to write  and debug the R code, to check the results and to draft and revise the text. The authors are responsible for the content.
